title: Relativity
subtitle: Events, clocks, energy and the limits of flat spacetime
prerequisites: Mathematical toolkit, Classical mechanics, Electricity & magnetism. Local mathematical bridges are taught before use; advanced topics retain their stated prerequisites.

lessons.title: An event is a where-and-when address
lessons.idea: An event is one occurrence; coordinates are the labels a chosen frame gives it.
body: A flash happens at one place and one time. That occurrence is an event. A reference frame supplies rulers and a grid of clocks so we can label the flash, rather than confusing it with when a distant observer sees it.

In one dimension write the address as (t,x). The coordinate x says where; t says what the local synchronized clock reads. A second observer may assign different numbers to the same event. Changing labels does not create a second flash.
An inertial frame is one in which an isolated object moves at constant velocity. We start with ideal inertial frames and flat spacetime, not a rotating room or a gravitational field.
lessons.terms: t: coordinate time (s). Seconds on the local clock belonging to the selected frame. x: position coordinate (m). Signed distance from that frame’s chosen origin.

example.title: Follow one concrete case
steps: Choose a laboratory origin at a detector.
A flash at that detector when its clock reads 2 s has address (2 s,0 m).
A flash 3 m to its right at 2 s is a different event, (2 s,3 m), even if light from both reaches you together.

check.prompt: Two cameras receive light together from different distances. What can you infer?
options: Their reception events share a time in the stated frame; the emission times need not match.
The flashes were necessarily emitted together.
The two flashes were one event.
explanations: Correct. Different path lengths can require different travel times. Simultaneous reception therefore does not establish simultaneous emission.
Travel times can differ.
Different emission locations mean different events.

apply.title: Explain a changed situation
apply.text: How would you find an emission time from a reception time?
apply.answer: Account for the light travel time in a specified frame. The time when light reaches your eye is not automatically the coordinate time of its emission.

lessons.limits: Ideal frame coordinates; real timing requires calibrated clocks and signal-delay corrections.

glossary.definition: A single physical occurrence at a location and time.
A system of rulers and clocks used to assign coordinates.

lessons.title: Set a distant clock using a round-trip signal
lessons.idea: Einstein synchronization assigns the midpoint of a round-trip light time to the distant reflection.
body: Put clock A at rest beside you and clock B at rest farther along the laboratory. A sends a flash, B reflects it immediately, and A receives it. We use the same local clock for departure and return.

If A reads t₁ on departure and t₂ on return, assign B’s reflection time tB=(t₁+t₂)/2. This is the Einstein synchronization convention for an inertial frame: the outgoing and returning vacuum light speeds are taken equal.

This is not an instruction to ignore apparatus delays. A waiting reflector adds a delay that must be measured and removed. A moving reflector does not define two stationary clocks in this simple procedure.
lessons.terms: t₁,t₂,tB: send, return and assigned reflection times (s). Subscripts label events, not powers; all readings use seconds. d: stationary one-way distance (m). Half the vacuum round-trip path length. c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

example.title: Follow one concrete case
steps: A sends at 2 μs and receives at 10 μs; μs means one millionth of a second.
The midpoint is (2+10)/2=6 μs, so set the reflection reading to 6 μs.
The round trip took 8 μs; with rounded c=3.00×10⁸ m/s, d=1200 m.

check.prompt: An immediate return arrives 4 μs later than before, while departure time is unchanged. How does the assigned reflection time change?
options: It does not change.
It increases by 2 μs.
It increases by 4 μs.
explanations: The measured midpoint has changed.
Correct. The assigned reflection time is the midpoint: adding 4 μs to the return time adds 4/2=2 μs to that midpoint.
Only half of the extra round-trip time belongs to the outward leg.

apply.title: Explain a changed situation
apply.text: Why not set B to the departure reading when the flash arrives?
apply.answer: The flash takes time to reach B. Midpoint assignment accounts for that travel time under the stated stationary, vacuum assumptions.

lessons.title: A moving source does not add to vacuum light speed
lessons.idea: Every inertial frame measures the same vacuum light speed using its own rulers and synchronized clocks.
body: A lamp moving past the laboratory emits a flash. The laboratory measures that flash travelling at c in vacuum. A frame at rest with the lamp also measures c, not c plus or minus the lamp’s speed.

The rulers and clocks used in each measurement matter. Keeping Newton’s rule that all frames share one time would conflict with this result. Special relativity changes the relationship between space and time measurements.

Light in glass travels differently from light in vacuum; c is not the speed of every wave in every material. This statement concerns local inertial measurements, not an arbitrary coordinate speed in gravity.
lessons.equation: distance travelled in vacuum = c × elapsed time
lessons.terms: c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding. distance travelled: length of a vacuum light path in one inertial frame (m). Use the path and elapsed time from the same frame. elapsed time: time between emission and arrival in that frame (s). Measured with synchronized clocks when events occur at different places.

options: c
explanations: Source velocity is not added to vacuum light speed.
That subtraction is a Galilean rule, not the vacuum light result.
Correct. Vacuum light invariance applies in the detector’s inertial frame regardless of the source velocity; the source speed is not added to c.

apply.title: Explain a changed situation
apply.text: Does this mean sound also has one speed in all inertial frames?
apply.answer: No. Sound propagates through matter, so its speed depends on the medium and its motion. Vacuum light invariance is a different physical statement.

lessons.limits: Vacuum, inertial measurements; material propagation and curved-spacetime coordinates need separate models.

lessons.title: Why subtracting velocities fails for light
lessons.idea: The Galilean rule is an excellent slow-motion approximation, but it cannot keep vacuum light speed invariant.
body: For everyday motion, a moving frame uses x′=x−vt and t′=t. A prime labels the moving frame; it does not mean a derivative here. The rule assumes both frames share the same elapsed time.
For a right-moving light pulse, x=ct. Substitution gives x′=(c−v)t′, so the Galilean rule predicts speed c−v. That disagrees with the vacuum light result whenever v is not zero.

The lesson is not that subtraction is bad arithmetic. One of the physical assumptions behind this coordinate rule must change. Lorentz transformations change both position and time while recovering this rule at small speed ratios.

Equality is the Galilean assumption, not the exact relativistic rule. u,u′: object velocities (m/s). Signed velocities in the corresponding frames. v: frame velocity along x (m/s). Positive means the primed frame moves toward increasing x in the unprimed frame. c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

lessons.title: The time carried by one clock
lessons.idea: Proper time is the elapsed reading of a clock that passes through both events.
body: A clock rides inside a spacecraft. Its tick at departure and tick at arrival lie on that clock’s path. The elapsed reading between them is proper time, written Δτ, with Greek tau.

A laboratory may assign a different coordinate time Δt between those same events using clocks at different locations. The difference Δ means final value minus initial value; it is not a separate unit.

For constant speed v in an inertial laboratory, Δτ=Δt√(1−v²/c²). A moving clock accumulates less time than the lab coordinate-time interval. This compares the same event pair, not arbitrary clocks photographed from far away.

Lab times assigned to the same two events. v: frame velocity along x (m/s). Positive means the primed frame moves toward increasing x in the unprimed frame. c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

steps: Let a clock move at 0.6c for a laboratory interval of 10 s.
The square-root factor is √(1−0.6²)=0.8.

explanations: That is division by 0.8 rather than multiplication.
Correct. For the same speed 0.6c, the factor remains √(1−0.6²)=0.8. The new reading is 20×0.8=16 s.
That would ignore the speed-dependent factor.

apply.text: Can two events at different places share one stationary lab clock?
apply.answer: No. A stationary lab clock stays at one place. Coordinate time can use a synchronized clock network; proper time belongs to a particular clock path through the events.

lessons.limits: Timelike clock path; constant velocity for this simple formula, negligible gravity.

lessons.title: A longer light path between ticks
lessons.idea: A transverse light clock gives time dilation because a moving frame sees a longer diagonal light path.
body: Imagine two mirrors separated vertically by distance L in a clock’s rest frame. One tick is a light round trip between them. In that frame the tick lasts 2L/c.

Watch the clock move horizontally. While the light crosses, the receiving mirror shifts sideways. For half a tick, the diagonal distance cΔt/2 has vertical side L and horizontal side vΔt/2. The Pythagorean rule relates their squares.

Solving gives Δt=γΔτ. The moving lab view has a longer light path and the same light speed, so it needs a longer coordinate time. This ideal light clock illustrates a general proper-time relation, not a defect unique to mirrors.
lessons.terms: c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding. v: frame velocity along x (m/s). Positive means the primed frame moves toward increasing x in the unprimed frame. γ: Lorentz factor (no unit). Greek gamma; γ=1/√(1−v²/c²), with |v|<c. √ means the positive square root. L: mirror separation transverse to motion (m). The perpendicular separation is unchanged by this boost. Δt,Δτ: lab tick time and clock-rest tick time (s). Δτ=2L/c. Squaring means multiplying a quantity by itself.

The ratio doubles.

explanations: Both light paths grow with the mirror spacing.

Correct. Both the rest light path and the lab diagonal light path scale with L. The ratio depends only on the unchanged speed through γ.

lessons.title: Measure both ends at the same lab time
lessons.idea: A moving object’s length uses simultaneous endpoint positions in the measuring frame.
body: Place a rod at rest in one frame. Its proper length L₀ is the separation of its ends measured there. The zero subscript labels the rest measurement.

To measure the moving rod in the lab, record both endpoint positions at the same lab time. Their difference is L=L₀/γ. Different frames disagree about which separated endpoint events are simultaneous.

This is not a claim that the rod feels squeezed. Its own rulers still measure L₀. A photograph also includes different light travel times, so its apparent shape is not automatically this simultaneous length.

Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

lessons.title: Same time in one frame is not same time in every frame
lessons.idea: Separated events simultaneous in one frame generally have different times in a moving frame.
body: Let frame S′ move in the positive x direction at speed v relative to S. For two events, their time difference transforms as Δt′=γ(Δt−vΔx/c²). The spatial separation contributes to the transformed time.

If S calls the events simultaneous, Δt=0. With v positive and the second event farther right, Δx positive, the second event has negative Δt′: it occurs earlier in S′. This is a statement about synchronized coordinate clocks, not delayed eyesight.
Events at the same position do not have this simultaneity offset. The disagreement concerns spatially separated event pairs and does not let a cause follow its own light-speed-or-slower effect.

Greek gamma; γ=1/√(1−v²/c²), with |v|<c. √ means the positive square root. c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

lessons.title: Check the speed before taking the square root
lessons.idea: The Lorentz factor is real and finite only for relative inertial-frame speeds smaller than c.
body: Write β=v/c, pronounced beta. This ratio has no unit because numerator and denominator are both speeds. Then γ=1/√(1−β²). The factor is at least 1.
At β=0, γ=1. As the speed magnitude approaches c, the denominator approaches zero and γ grows without bound. There is no inertial rest frame moving at c relative to the laboratory.

At a proposed speed greater than c, the square-root input becomes negative. That is a signal that this ordinary boost formula is outside its physical domain, not permission to make a faster-than-light frame.

lessons.title: Transform position and time together
lessons.idea: A Lorentz boost mixes an event’s position and time while leaving the event itself unchanged.
body: Align the axes of S and S′. Let the origins coincide when both read zero, and let S′ move at velocity v along positive x. These choices fix the signs and remove arbitrary origin shifts.
The transformation is x′=γ(x−vt) and t′=γ(t−vx/c²). Apply both formulas to the same event. Transforming x but retaining the old t would combine incompatible coordinate systems.
It can help to use ct as a length instead of t: ct′=γ(ct−βx). Now both terms inside each subtraction have metres as units. Divide ct′ by c only when you need seconds.

lessons.title: Combine speeds without outrunning light
lessons.idea: Relativistic velocity addition transforms both distance and elapsed time.
body: An object has velocity u′ in S′, while S′ moves at v relative to S. For motion along the same line, its S velocity is u=(u′+v)/(1+u′v/c²). The denominator matters when speeds are large.
The rule follows by dividing transformed small position changes by transformed small time changes. It is not obtained by clipping an ordinary sum at c.
If u′=c, numerator and denominator cancel to give u=c. If both speeds are much smaller than c, the product u′v/c² is tiny and the denominator is nearly 1, recovering ordinary addition.

lessons.title: Subtract the spatial square from the time square
lessons.idea: The spacetime interval stays unchanged under Lorentz boosts even though its separate coordinate terms change.
body: For two events in one spatial dimension define s²=(cΔt)²−(Δx)². This course uses the time-positive sign convention. Another book may reverse every sign; the physics is unchanged if it stays consistent.

The interval is not the ordinary distance on a sheet of paper: there is a minus sign. It can be positive, zero, or negative. The notation s² names the signed interval and does not promise a positive ordinary square.
A Lorentz transformation preserves this combination. For events joined by an inertial clock, s²=c²Δτ², linking the invariant to a measured proper time.

Δx: position difference (m). Use the same event ordering as Δt. Δτ: proper time on a straight timelike path (s). For positive interval, Δτ=√s²/c. c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

lessons.title: Three kinds of event separation
lessons.idea: The sign of the interval tells whether a light-speed-or-slower connection is possible.
body: If s² is positive, the events are timelike separated. Their spatial separation is smaller than the distance light could travel in their time separation. A sublight clock can connect them in the appropriate time direction.

If s² is zero, the separation is null, also called lightlike. An ideal vacuum light signal can connect them. If s² is negative, it is spacelike: no signal moving at or below c can cross the gap in the available time.
This classification is frame-independent because the interval is invariant. A change of observer cannot turn an impossible causal connection into an ordinary light signal.

Spacelike pairs are different. Their order may reverse under a boost because no light-speed-or-slower message can connect them. Relativity of simultaneity does not therefore imply that a message can arrive before it is sent.
For a spacelike pair, setting Δt′=0 gives v=c²Δt/Δx. Its magnitude is below c precisely because |Δx| exceeds c|Δt|. A slightly larger boost can reverse the coordinate order.

lessons.title: Add the time on each stretch of a journey
lessons.idea: A travelling clock’s total time is the sum of its proper-time increments along its path.
body: When a clock changes velocity, one constant-speed formula cannot describe the whole trip. Divide the path into segments on which the speed is constant and calculate each segment’s proper time.
For segment i, Δτᵢ=Δtᵢ√(1−vᵢ²/c²). Add these increments. The symbol Σ means sum over the listed segments; the subscript i labels a segment, not a new unit.

For smoothly varying speed the sum becomes an integral. Here we use piecewise constant motion and explicitly idealize the short changes between segments. Proper time depends on the path, not just the endpoint coordinates.

Each segment uses the same inertial lab frame. vᵢ: lab velocity on segment i (m/s). Its sign may change; its square sets the segment factor. Σᵢ: sum over segments (no unit). Add one contribution for each segment. c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

Let the traveller move at 0.6c for 5 lab seconds outward and 5 lab seconds inward. Ignoring a brief turnaround, it accumulates 8 s; the lab clock accumulates 10 s.

The paths are not symmetric: the traveller switches inertial frames to return. Acceleration marks this asymmetry; proper time is calculated along the whole path.

For recession speed v>0, the frequency ratio is freceived/femitted=√[(1−β)/(1+β)], where β=v/c. It is below 1: a redshift. For approach use the opposite sign of β, giving a ratio above 1.

This is the longitudinal relativistic Doppler effect, not just the gamma factor. A transverse or changing geometry needs its own angle-aware formula. Frequency is measured locally by each observer’s clock.

lessons.title: A changing velocity needs a changing local rest frame
lessons.idea: An accelerating observer has momentarily comoving inertial frames, not one global inertial rest frame.
body: At one instant, choose an inertial frame moving with an accelerating clock’s current velocity. The clock is momentarily at rest there. A moment later its velocity changes, so a different comoving frame is needed.

For straight-line motion, proper acceleration α is the acceleration measured by an accelerometer carried with the object. Coordinate acceleration a=dv/dt is the velocity change per lab second. They satisfy α=γ³a for one-dimensional motion.

An accelerating rocket can maintain a constant accelerometer reading while its lab coordinate acceleration decreases as its speed rises. Neither quantity permits a massive clock to reach c after a finite amount of finite proper acceleration.

lessons.title: Momentum grows faster than speed
lessons.idea: For a massive particle, relativistic momentum is mass times velocity times the Lorentz factor.
body: At everyday speeds we use momentum p=mv. At large speed, use p=γmv, where m is invariant mass, sometimes called rest mass. We do not redefine mass as a speed-dependent quantity in this course.

The sign of momentum follows the sign of velocity in one dimension. Gamma increases the magnitude and grows without bound as speed approaches c. Adding momentum therefore produces smaller and smaller speed increases near c.
For an isolated interaction, add signed momentum components in one frame before and after. A large gamma is not a reason to abandon momentum conservation.

lessons.title: Separate rest energy from motion energy
lessons.idea: Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is the excess above rest energy.
body: A free massive particle has total energy E=γmc². Even in its rest frame it has rest energy E₀=mc². Kinetic energy K=E−E₀=(γ−1)mc² is zero at rest.

Energy does not need to be “used up” just because a particle has rest mass. Converting part of a system’s mass into escaping energy requires an allowed physical process and conservation of all relevant quantities.
At speeds much smaller than c, γ−1 is approximately v²/(2c²), giving the familiar K≈mv²/2. The approximation fails near c.

lessons.title: Check energy and momentum as a pair
lessons.idea: The combination E²−p²c² equals the squared rest energy of a free particle or isolated system.
body: Energy and momentum change when you change inertial frames, but they cannot change independently. They obey E²−p²c²=m²c⁴ for a particle with invariant mass m.
In three dimensions p² means px²+py²+pz², the squared momentum magnitude. In this one-dimensional lesson p is a signed component, and squaring removes its sign.

For a whole system, use total energy and total vector momentum first, then compute its invariant mass. Adding individual particle masses instead generally misses internal kinetic or interaction energy.

Small-particle energies are often written in electronvolts. One electronvolt (eV) is the energy gained by a charge of one positive elementary-charge magnitude through a potential drop of one volt: 1 eV=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J. One mega-electronvolt (MeV) is one million eV. Dividing an energy by c gives a momentum unit, MeV/c; dividing by c² gives a mass unit, MeV/c². These are different physical quantities, not interchangeable labels.

MeV/c, MeV/c²: energy-derived momentum and mass units (momentum and mass, respectively). Divide energy by c for momentum, or by c² for mass. A rest energy of 12 MeV corresponds to a mass of 12 MeV/c².

lessons.title: Zero rest mass does not mean zero energy
lessons.idea: A photon has zero invariant mass but carries energy and momentum.
body: For a photon in vacuum, m=0 in the energy-momentum relation. This gives E=|p|c. Momentum still has direction; a left-moving photon has negative p in a right-positive axis.
Photon energy is E=hf, where h is Planck’s constant and f is local frequency. Higher frequency means more energy per photon, not necessarily more photons.

There is no inertial frame at rest with a photon. Do not put v=c into a massive-particle formula and try to multiply an infinite gamma by zero mass. The massless energy-momentum relation is the appropriate statement.

body: A particle’s four-momentum is P=(E/c,px,py,pz). Each entry then has momentum units. The word “four” counts one energy-related component plus three spatial ones.
For an isolated collision, add each component before and after: total energy and each signed momentum component are conserved. Never add momentum magnitudes when directions differ.
In one-dimensional examples we can display (E,pc) instead, so both entries use energy units. That is a convenient rescaling for arithmetic; label it clearly rather than silently changing units.

A system consisting only of perfectly parallel photons has zero invariant mass and no such rest frame. The formula would require V=c, outside the ordinary frame domain.

lessons.idea: When motion energy is trapped inside a merged object, its invariant mass includes that energy.
body: Two equal particles approach with equal opposite momenta and stick together without radiation escaping. The initial centre-of-momentum frame is also the final object’s rest frame.
If each incoming particle has mass m and Lorentz factor γ, their total energy is 2γmc². Conservation gives final mass M=2γm. It exceeds 2m because internal energy remains in the final object.

This does not violate mass-energy accounting. The sum of separate rest masses need not be conserved; total four-momentum is. If energy escapes as radiation, include that radiation before computing the remaining object’s mass.

body: Consider a photon of energy E striking a stationary target of mass M. The initial system has total energy Mc²+E and momentum magnitude E/c. Its invariant energy squared is M²c⁴+2Mc²E.
At the kinematic threshold for a specified final total rest mass Mf, the products have no relative motion in their centre-of-momentum frame. Set the initial invariant equal to Mf²c⁴ and solve for E.
This gives E=((Mf²−M²)c²)/(2M). It is a minimum allowed by energy and momentum, not a promise the reaction occurs. Charge, other conserved quantities, and interaction rules must also permit it.

lessons.idea: A frame change can alter measured charge density and current density while preserving charge conservation.
body: Charge density ρ says how much charge occupies a unit volume in the chosen frame. Current density jx says how much charge crosses a unit area per second along x. Both depend on how motion and simultaneous volume are measured.

The pair transforms as ρ′=γ(ρ−vjx/c²) and jx′=γ(jx−vρ). This is the one-dimensional part of the four-current transformation. A neutral distribution in one frame need not have zero local charge density in another if it carries current.

Total charge of a complete isolated system is invariant. Do not confuse that with the density in a selected slice of a wire; different frames choose different simultaneous slices. Charge continuity remains valid in every inertial frame.

lessons.title: Electric and magnetic fields depend on the frame
lessons.idea: A Lorentz boost can mix perpendicular electric and magnetic field components.
body: An electric field and a magnetic field are not two unrelated substances. They are frame-dependent parts of the electromagnetic field. Different observers can assign different E and B while agreeing on physical outcomes after all quantities are transformed.

For a boost along positive x, the perpendicular components obey Ey′=γ(Ey−vBz) and Bz′=γ(Bz−vEy/c²). The signs here are fixed by the chosen axes and boost convention; other components require their matching formulas.

If S has only a positive Ey field and no magnetic field, S′ measures an enhanced Ey′ and a negative Bz′. A moving test charge also has a transformed velocity, so comparing forces requires more than changing the field alone.

lessons.title: Four-vector means a transformation rule
lessons.idea: A four-vector is a set of four components that transform together in the Lorentz pattern.
body: The name does not mean “any list with four numbers.” The event-displacement set (cΔt,Δx,Δy,Δz) is a four-vector because a boost mixes its time and parallel-space components in the Lorentz way.
Four-momentum (E/c,px,py,pz) follows the same pattern. For a boost along x, E′/c=γ(E/c−βpx) and px′=γ(px−βE/c), while the transverse momentum components are unchanged.

This shared transformation structure lets us build invariant combinations and conservation laws. The numerical components are not invariant individually; it is the object and its transformation relationship that are meaningful.

lessons.title: The law keeps its form, not every number
lessons.idea: A Lorentz-covariant law has the same mathematical relationship in every inertial frame.
body: Covariant means the quantities transform together so the law retains its form. For example, if total four-momentum before an isolated collision equals total four-momentum after, boosting both sides preserves the equality.

This does not mean each observer measures the same energy or force. Those components can differ. It means the transformed observer can use the same physical law with their own consistently transformed data.

A formula that assumes a special rest frame can still be a useful material model, but its domain must say so. For example, a medium’s rest-frame properties should not be inserted unchanged into every moving-frame expression.

lessons.title: Free fall removes local weight, not all gravity
lessons.idea: A sufficiently small freely falling laboratory locally behaves like an inertial laboratory, apart from tidal effects.
body: Imagine a sealed box falling freely. An unsupported object inside falls with it, so it floats relative to the box. An accelerometer carried by the falling box reads zero in ideal free fall, even though its position changes relative to the ground.

A box held at rest on the ground is not freely falling: the ground pushes upward. Its accelerometer registers that support. Weightlessness means absence of this support force, not necessarily absence of a gravitational field.

The equivalence principle is local. Two separated falling objects can accelerate differently because gravity varies across space. These tidal effects cannot generally be removed throughout a finite region by choosing one freely falling frame.

lessons.title: Higher stationary clocks can tick faster
lessons.idea: In a weak static gravitational field, a clock at higher potential accumulates slightly more time.
body: Compare two stationary clocks in a weak, slowly varying gravitational environment. If clock 2 is at potential Φ₂ and clock 1 at Φ₁, their small fractional rate difference is approximately(Φ₂−Φ₁)/c².

Near Earth over a modest height change Δh, the potential difference is approximately gΔh, with g treated constant. A higher clock then ticks faster relative to a lower stationary clock. This is a gravitational effect, not a relative-velocity time dilation.

The approximation requires potential differences small compared with c² and a suitable static comparison. Accurate satellite timing also includes velocity, Earth’s shape, and other corrections; this is not a complete navigation model.

lessons.title: Free paths need not be straight on a global map
lessons.idea: In general relativity, an ideal freely falling test body follows a geodesic of spacetime.
body: A geodesic is the path selected by spacetime geometry for free motion. In a small freely falling laboratory it looks locally straight. On a large coordinate map it can curve, just as a route that is locally straight on a curved surface need not look straight on a flat drawing.

The surface analogy is only a guide. Spacetime includes time and a metric with a different sign structure from ordinary surface distances. Massive particles follow timelike geodesics; light follows null geodesics.
Neighboring geodesics may approach or separate. Their relative behavior expresses tidal gravity. An orbit is therefore not evidence that a freely falling astronaut must feel a support force.

Timelike intervals are positive in this course’s sign convention. 0: null interval value (m²). Light has zero spacetime interval, not zero spatial travel distance.

lessons.idea: Special relativity works locally, but extended gravitational comparisons generally require general relativity.
body: Special relativity assumes flat spacetime for its global inertial-frame formulas. It can describe acceleration in flat spacetime; acceleration alone is not proof of spacetime curvature.

Gravity’s tidal effects indicate that one flat description may fail across the region being studied. A sufficiently small freely falling laboratory still permits local special-relativistic measurements.

Before using a formula, state the size of the region, the required timing precision, and whether gravitational variation matters. Small effects can be essential for a precision clock even when a rough everyday estimate ignores them.

Write a short measurement sentence beside each answer: “the lab network assigns this interval” or “the travelling clock records this elapsed time.” That sentence can expose an event-pair mix-up before the arithmetic begins.

lessons.title: A report of arrival reaches the origin later
lessons.idea: Signal reception time includes the travel time of the report as well as the traveller’s journey.
body: A spacecraft leaves the lab origin, reaches a stationary detector, and immediately sends a light pulse back to the origin. There are three events: departure A, turnaround or signal emission B, and reception C at the origin.
In the lab, A-to-B takes D/v. The return pulse B-to-C takes D/c because the detector and receiving origin are fixed a distance D apart. Thus the origin’s elapsed time A-to-C is D/v+D/c.
The origin clock visits A and C, so this reception interval is also its proper time. The spacecraft’s A-to-B proper time is a different quantity. Neither time should replace the other.

lessons.title: Check a collision with two independent totals
lessons.idea: A proposed collision outcome must pass energy, momentum and invariant-mass checks together.
body: Two photons approach along opposite directions with energies 9 MeV and 4 MeV. Select both photons as the initial system and use positive x along the 9 MeV photon. Total energy is 13 MeV and total momentum times c is 5 MeV.
The system rest energy is√(13²−5²)=12 MeV. If an allowed interaction traps all energy into one final composite object, that object has invariant mass 12 MeV/c² and lab speed(5/13)c.

The final object is not stationary in the lab, because the incoming momenta do not cancel. Its rest energy is smaller than its lab total energy; the difference is lab kinetic energy. Reaction feasibility still needs more than this kinematic accounting.
lessons.terms: M: final composite invariant mass (kg or MeV/c²). MeV/c² denotes the mass whose rest energy is the stated MeV value. Etotal: total lab energy (MeV). Mega-electronvolt is an energy unit;1 MeV=1.602176634×10⁻¹³ J. ptotal c: total momentum times c (MeV). Signed along the chosen x axis. V: final object lab velocity (m/s). Must remain below c for a positive invariant mass. c: vacuum light speed (m/s). Exactly 299792458 metres per second; use 3.00×10⁸ m/s only where the example requests rounding.

lessons.title: Know what the introductory map does not solve
lessons.idea: Further relativity requires geometric tools, physical assumptions and validation beyond a few familiar formulas.
body: You can now distinguish frame-dependent coordinates from invariant intervals, track proper time, and conserve four-momentum. These are foundations, not a complete general-relativity course.

A fuller gravity calculation specifies a spacetime metric, uses tensor calculus to compare quantities across coordinates, solves geodesic or field equations, and checks the assumptions against observations. The stress-energy tensor describes energy, momentum and stresses that enter Einstein’s field equations.

Before choosing that larger machinery, ask whether the question is local and approximately flat, a weak-field clock comparison, or a genuinely curved-spacetime problem. State the precision and what has been neglected. A correct limited model is more useful than an impressive equation used outside its scope.
lessons.equation: model choice = physical regime + required precision + stated assumptions
lessons.terms: physical regime: the conditions being described (no unit). Examples: flat spacetime, weak static gravity, or strong curved spacetime. required precision: acceptable error scale (stated units or fractional ratio). Choose the error target before deciding which effects can be ignored. stated assumptions: conditions needed for the model (no unit). These are part of the answer, not optional decoration.
